## some notes based on a lit review via Claude on recongition memory and response bias ##

This might be relevant for interpreting the threshold effects for novel > learned/famous.

In a yes/no recognition task, participants systematically set a more liberal criterion for "old" (familiar) responses than for "new" (novel) responses — they are more willing to say "yes, I've seen this" than "no, I haven't". This is the mirror effect in recognition memory: hits and correct rejections trade off asymmetrically because the decision criteria for the two responses are not equal.
Relevant references:

Glanzer & Adams (1985) — the original mirror effect paper, showing that easier items produce both more hits and fewer false alarms, creating asymmetric response criteria
Stretch & Wixted (1998) — signal detection analysis of the mirror effect, directly relevant to criterion placement for old vs new responses
Rotello, Macmillan & Reeder (2004) — demonstrates that old/new recognition involves asymmetric criteria even when controlling for item difficulty
Ratcliff, Sheu & Gronlund (1992) — specifically links diffusion model parameters to recognition memory criteria, bridging EAM and recognition memory literatures
Verde & Rotello (2007) — shows that the criterion for "new" responses is systematically higher than for "old" responses across a range of conditions

The Ratcliff et al. (1992) paper is probably the most directly relevant given your EAM framing — it explicitly discusses how threshold asymmetries emerge in recognition memory tasks using a drift diffusion framework, which maps directly onto your LBA threshold results.
